reason: GENUINE elapsed-time observation, and the only one left in this file (the other three -- 1200ms, 600ms, 300ms -- became waitUntil polls in the same change). This one asserts an ABSENCE: after SIGTERM, no further 'started' event ever appears. An absence has no arrival to poll for, so waitUntil cannot express it; the only way to evidence that nothing happened is to let time pass and look. It is also the SAFE direction of wall-clock dependence -- extra elapsed time on a loaded runner makes this check MORE thorough, never flakier, which is the exact opposite of every sleep removed elsewhere here. Note the file is in bunfig pathIgnorePatterns and executes in no CI lane today, so its live blast radius is zero either way.

The 60-second hang is the fixture the sandbox is asked to kill, so removing it would delete the experiment rather than the ambient dependency. Same distinction as .claude/rules/no-binary-in-proof-lineage.md draws for the wasm modules: the thing under test is not evidence. The test's own verdict comes from the sandbox's kill, which is observed, not timed.

LIVE INTEGRATION against a real long-running worker process, and the sleep is the module's own `sleep(ms)` helper rather than an assertion. The file's subject is keep-alive behaviour over real elapsed time -- a keep-alive that fires instantly is not a keep-alive -- so wall-clock is the observable, not a stand-in for one. Kept under the count pin so a SECOND timer in this file still has to be argued for; the exemption is for the one helper, not for the file.

The match is inside a STRING LITERAL handed to a spawned process: --work-arg 'setTimeout(() => {}, 4000)'. The slow child IS the fixture the cascade is asked to time out on, so removing the delay would delete the experiment rather than an ambient dependency. The test's verdict comes from the runner's own timeout decision, which is observed, not timed.

THE DELAY IS THE CONDITION UNDER TEST, not a stand-in for an event. The subject is a multi-byte UTF-8 character cut in half across two TCP writes -- something a network does on its own at unpredictable offsets. Doing it deliberately is what makes the failure REPRODUCIBLE; a same-tick second write would not fragment and the test would silently stop testing anything. 15ms is a packet boundary, not a settling period, and the assertion is on the reassembled string rather than on elapsed time. Kept under the count pin so a SECOND timer in this file still has to be argued for.

NOT THE HARNESS'S CLOCK -- THE SUBJECT UNDER TEST, the same distinction the subprocess-sandbox row below draws. All three matches are inside STRING LITERALS that are the source of spawned stub processes: two in `['-e', 'setInterval(()=>{},1000)']` handed to a detached grandchild, and one in the stub body. Their job is to keep a process ALIVE so that the session's tree-kill has something to kill; deleting them would delete the experiment rather than an ambient dependency. The tests' own verdicts come from `waitUntil(() => !isAlive(pid))` -- the death is OBSERVED, never timed -- which is what the two real 250ms poll-sleeps in this file were replaced with in the same change, and those two were the file's only failures on a developer laptop. Count pinned at 3 so a FOURTH timer here still has to be argued for; the exemption is for these stub fixtures, not for the file.

GENUINE elapsed-time observation, and it is the assertion rather than a delay before one. The test proves two follow-ups at dop 2 OVERLAP instead of serialising: it records Date.now() either side and asserts elapsed < sleepMs * 2. Overlap is a claim ABOUT DURATION, so there is no arrival to poll for -- waitUntil can tell you both finished, not that they ran at once. The `setTimeout` the audit sees is not in the test at all: it is inside a generated child-process stub (`session.cjs`) that stands in for a model session, so the test file's source carries the call while the delay happens in another process. NOTED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the margin is 2x on a 1500 ms sleep, which is the UNSAFE direction -- a loaded runner can push an overlapping run past 3000 ms and fail a correct implementation. The load-independent form is a barrier: have both stubs signal STARTED and assert both started before either finished, which needs no clock. Worth doing when this test is next touched.
